reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents MemeCore and its $M token through a presenter-led discussion of project information, market figures, website navigation, exchange listings, and community links. The promotional material includes reported figures, a buyback post, and a trading-competition promotion alongside risk and paid-production disclosures, without establishing guaranteed returns, required private data, completed rewards, or that the buybacks occurred.

opening.argument: Judge the return claim together with the requested action. The presenter highlights a reported 140 percent monthly rise, then tells viewers to follow the website link and “get in on this.” The site shown in the video has a “BUY $M” button, and its exchange section directs visitors toward trading. That sequence turns past appreciation into a reason to acquire the token. It does not promise the same return again, but it uses the return to make the purchase invitation persuasive.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the cited price figures describe past performance and that the speaker acknowledges risk. But neither point separates the figures from his invitation to “get in on this.” A conditional hope for another meme season still supplies a reason to act now, especially when the linked project site presents a purchase route. The issue is how the figures are used, not whether the speaker guarantees a return.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The invitation and purchase button establish promotion, but not a deceptive return promise. The speaker dates the reported price to the time of recording and describes a possible meme-season recovery as “maybe.” He also tells viewers to understand cryptocurrency risk. Those qualifications matter: the cited material shows enthusiasm for a token and a way to buy it, not evidence that buying will reproduce its past gains.

opening.argument: Look at the cumulative pitch. The presenter says the token has risen while much of the market has fallen and calls himself bullish. The video also shows a project post claiming weekly $M buybacks, a trading promotion offering a share of 40,000 USDT, and a prominent purchase button. Together, those signals invite viewers to see recent gains, continuing support, and a trading reward as reasons to enter. The material shown does not verify future appreciation or completed buybacks; that gap matters when the optimistic signals accompany a buying route.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense notes that buybacks are not shown to have occurred and that rewards are not shown to have been paid. That is precisely why those claims should not receive evidentiary weight as established benefits. Yet they appear alongside the speaker's bullish assessment and a visible path to buying $M. A general warning about crypto risk does not substantiate the promotional claims or erase their combined pull.

The sampled frame presents a buyback post and a trading competition as claims, not verified future returns to a purchaser. The presenter expressly discusses cryptocurrency risk, and the description warns that an investor can lose all their money. The evidence supports promotional market commentary with disclosed risk, not a demonstrated promise that buying $M will pay off.

opening.argument: This is more than a neutral walkthrough of a chart. After reporting the token's price and gains, the presenter tells viewers to check the website link and “get in on this.” The project site displayed on screen offers “BUY $M,” while its exchange section invites trading. The description also discloses that the presenter is paid to make these videos. Read together, the market figures and website tour function as a paid promotional path toward acquiring a token whose recent appreciation is emphasized.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense calls this a presenter-led discussion of market figures, links, and project information. Those are the very components of the solicitation: favorable performance is presented before viewers are directed to the project site. The payment disclosure makes the promotional role explicit. It is relevant that returns are not guaranteed, but the absence of a guarantee does not make an invitation to participate merely informational.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion is not, by itself, evidence of a scam. The speaker discloses that he is paid, warns that cryptocurrency investing can lose money, and frames the hoped-for recovery as a possibility. His discussion includes reported price movement rather than a guaranteed gain from purchasing. The opening accurately identifies a promotional pathway, but it does not show that the reported figures are false or that viewers are promised a return.
